title: Ice storms don't follow the snow: where FEMA rates the risk Very High
seoTitle: Ice Storm Risk 2026: FEMA Ratings for 300 U.S. Cities, From Dallas to Oklahoma City
description: 57 of 300 U.S. cities sit in counties FEMA rates Very High for ice storm risk, including Dallas, with just 23 freezing nights a year. What to check in a home.
ctaTitle: Check a specific home before ice season
ctaText: Enter the address to see its census-tract ice storm, winter weather and cold wave ratings, plus rail and road traffic nearby.
lead: Snow piles up in Bismarck and Denver, but an ice storm is a different hazard: freezing rain that glazes trees and power lines. Using FEMA's National Risk Index and NOAA climate normals for the 300 cities we track, here is where ice storm risk rates highest, why the list looks nothing like a snowfall map, and what to check in a house before the season starts.
sources: FEMA National Risk Index: Understanding Scores and Ratings

title: Nashville's flight-path fight: what the federal noise map shows, and what it misses
seoTitle: Nashville Airport Noise 2026: BNA Flight Path Changes and What the Federal Noise Map Shows
description: Metro Council backed South Nashville residents on BNA flight paths. USDOT's map: 22% of Nashville residents live where aircraft noise reaches 45 dB or more.

image.author: Carol M. Highsmith
image.alt: Nashville, Tennessee skyline seen across the city

ctaTitle: Check aircraft noise at a specific address
ctaText: Enter the address to see modeled road, rail and aircraft noise at the home, plus the nearest rail crossing and the busiest road nearby.
lead: Nashville's Metro Council has sided with South Nashville neighbors who say new departure routes from Nashville International Airport put a steady stream of jets over their homes. Here is what happened, what the federal noise map shows for Nashville, and why a buyer should not rely on that map alone near BNA.

title: Frozen-pipe season: where freezing nights are routine, and where a rare freeze does more damage
seoTitle: Frozen Pipes 2026: Freezing Nights in 300 U.S. Cities (NOAA) and Where Rare Freezes Hit Hardest
description: NOAA normals for 300 U.S. cities: Anchorage averages 204 freezing nights a year, Houston about 4. Why rare-freeze cities can be the riskier place for pipes, and what to check before buying.

image.author: Tomwsulcer
image.alt: Large icicles hanging from a roof gutter after a hard freeze

ctaTitle: Check a specific home before winter
ctaText: Enter the address to see its census-tract cold wave, winter storm and flood ratings, plus rail and road traffic nearby.
lead: Freezing weather is a known quantity in Fargo and a surprise in Houston. Using NOAA climate normals and FEMA's National Risk Index for the 300 cities we track, here is where freezing nights are common, where they are rare but still dangerous, and what a homebuyer should check before winter.

title: Kent's new quiet zone: 8 BNSF crossings, 42 trains a day, and records that have not caught up
seoTitle: Kent, WA Railroad Quiet Zone (2026): 8 BNSF Crossings, Night Trains and Accident History
description: Kent, Washington's quiet zone took effect in late August 2026 on eight BNSF crossings. FRA records: 21 night trains per crossing, 36 passenger trains a day, 10 incidents since 2021.

image.author: SounderBruce
image.alt: Sounder commuter train at Kent Station, Washington

lead: Kent spent about $3.5 million to stop routine train horns at eight downtown crossings on the BNSF mainline. The federal crossing records show why residents asked for it, and that the paperwork still says otherwise.
sources: Kent Reporter / Auburn Reporter: Kent receives approval for Quiet Zone along railroad tracks (June 19, 2026)
FRA Highway-Rail Crossing Inventory (Form 71), revision of Oct 12, 2026
FRA Highway-Rail Accident Reports (Form 57), Jan 2021 to Aug 2026

title: Which U.S. cities are loudest? Road, rail and airplane noise where people actually live
seoTitle: Noisiest U.S. Cities for Traffic, Train and Airplane Noise: 299 Cities Ranked by Residents Exposed
description: USDOT's national noise map, matched to 2020 census population: in Newark 20% of residents live where transportation noise averages 55 dB or more. The median city: 2.9%. Full ranking and what it means for a home search.

image.author: Transpoman
image.alt: Concrete noise wall along I-95 at the end of a residential street in Pelham Manor, New York

lead: Every city has a highway, a rail line or an airport. What differs is how many people live next to them. We matched the federal transportation noise map to where residents of 299 cities live, and the spread is wider than you might expect.

ctaText: The report shows the modeled road, rail and aircraft noise at the home, plus the nearest crossing, train counts and road traffic.

title: St. Louis train horns: the quiet zone is coming back. Here is what the federal records show
seoTitle: St. Louis Quiet Zone Reinstated (Nov 2026): Which Crossings, How Many Night Trains
description: St. Louis lost its railroad quiet zone in September 2026 and is getting it back in mid-November. FRA records: 138 of 147 crossings flagged quiet zone, 99 with night trains.

image.author: Harvey Henkelmann
image.alt: Nathan M5 five-chime locomotive air horn

lead: After about two months of horns at every crossing, St. Louis says routine train horns will stop again by mid-November. We matched the news against the federal crossing inventory: which lines are affected, how many trains run at night, and why a quiet-zone flag on paper is not a guarantee.
sources: St. Louis Public Radio: Train horns to stop sounding in St. Louis (Nov 6, 2026)
FRA Highway-Rail Crossing Inventory (Form 71), revision of Nov 2, 2026
FRA train horn rule and quiet zones
